note: W1-LIBRARY round 3. Six texts about one afternoon in 3E 391, written so the province has a partisan military history that argues about how a thing was won — the thing RI-LOR03 §2 T7 asks for and the corpus did not have. They engage the Ford material already in the library (a-short-account-of-the-pacification's 200/49 and its appendix; the-account-the-marsh-keeps's 151-against-a-dozen; the-drowned-ford's woman with a sluice gate) and none of them settles it. The Office minute is the load-bearing one: it establishes, in the Office's own hand, that the sentence the sixth issue of the drill book rests section 9 on has no paper behind it, and that the Office knows and has declined to correct it. Nothing in the game adjudicates. The 42-against-151 arithmetic on the muster leaf is not confirmed by any other document and is not meant to be.

books.title: The Relief of the Reman Ford: An Account Assembled From the Cohort's Own Papers, Against the Received One
books.author: Prefect Ancus Meline, on the staff at Gideon, who was 4 years old in 3E 391 and says so on the first page
books.unreliability: A serious historian doing serious work in the service of a conclusion he settled on before he opened the file. Every document he cites is real and his reading of each one is defensible and the accumulation is a case rather than an account. He never once considers that a fight on the near bank and a flood two days later could both have happened and neither have caused the other.

contradicts.on: whether there was a fight at the ford before the water came

books.text:
I was 4 years old in 3E 391 and I put that at the head of this so that no reader has to wonder. I was not there. Nobody who writes about the ford was there. Every account of that day in the province, including the one the Office prints, is somebody arranging paper.

I have arranged the paper differently and I think I have arranged it better, and here is the paper.

I. WHAT THE RECEIVED ACCOUNT SAYS.

Tribune Vell's *Short Account*, which is issued to every officer at the schools, gives the whole matter in a paragraph. A column of the Ninth moved inland to relieve a survey party. It was lost crossing at the old Reman ford in the dry season. Two hundred at muster, 49 at the far bank. Cause: a flood surge.

No enemy. No engagement. An accident of water, in a province where water has accidents.

The province tells it as a woman opening the fish-weirs upstream, and Vell answers that with an appendix of arithmetic on the volume of the weir ponds, and the arithmetic is right, and I will come back to it.

II. WHAT IS IN THE COHORT'S OWN PAPERS, WHICH VELL DID NOT READ.

Vell wrote at Anvil from the Office's file. The cohort's day-books are at Gideon in a room nobody goes into and they are not in the Office's file, and I have read the surviving leaves of the relief column's book, and they do not describe an accident.

They describe 3 days.

*The first day.* Twelve miles, no incident, the column complaining about the heat. The clerk notes that the water was low and that the survey party's last message had been 9 days old.

*The second day.* The column halted on the near bank at the middle of the afternoon and did not cross. The entry is 4 words and the 4 words are the reason I have written this book: *halted near bank. line formed.*

A column does not form line to cross a river. A column forms column to cross a river. A line is formed facing something.

*The third day.* The surge. The entry for the third day is in a different hand, is much longer, and is the entry every account since has quoted, and it says the water came up out of a dry channel and took the middle of the column while it was on the causeway.

III. THE ARGUMENT.

Set the second day beside the third and the received account cannot stand as written.

If there was nothing on the far bank, why did the column stand to on the near one for an afternoon and a night, in the heat, in a season when every officer's whole ambition is to be out of the sun by the fourth hour? Vell's account has 200 men going down to a ford and walking into water. The book has them stopping short of it, forming a line, and waiting.

I say: there was something on the far bank on the second day. I say the line was formed because a line was needed. I say the reason no engagement appears in the returns is that the Office was assembling a report about a drowning while the province was already telling a story about a woman, and an engagement in the middle of it would have raised the question of who the engagement was with — and the answer to that question was, and remains, that the Empire does not know who lives 2 days inland.

IV. THE FIGURES.

The received figures are 200 at muster and 49 at the far bank. The province gives the dead as 151 in our books and as a dozen in theirs, and there is a woman at Lilmoth who has told several people that the loss was the carts.

Take those three claims together, which nobody does, because each side quotes only the one that suits it.

151 dead is 200 less 49. It is not a count. It is a subtraction, and the subtraction assumes that every man not at the far bank was in the water, and there is no reason on earth to assume that of a column that had formed line on the near bank the day before. Men who were on the near bank when the surge came were on the near bank afterwards. They are not dead. They are on the wrong side of a river with no bridge, and they walked out, and they were entered at the wrong depot, and that is how an army loses 100 men on paper.

A dozen dead is the province's figure and I do not think it is a lie either. I think it is a count of the bodies that came ashore where the weir people could see them.

And the carts. I have found the loss return. The loss return gives 11 waggons and their teams as a total loss, in a column whose whole reason for going inland was that a survey party could not carry its own instruments home.

V. WHERE THIS LEAVES SECTION 9.

I come to the practical matter, since I am on the staff and not in a library.

The fourth issue of the Standing Instruction rests its rule on the line in standing water on the conduct of the men at the ford: that the line held for an afternoon and that those who died were those who broke rearward. The sixth issue repeats it. Every serjeant in this province has had that sentence read at him.

If I am right, the sentence is nearly true and is being used for the wrong thing. A line was formed and it did hold, for an afternoon, on a dry near bank, against something, at a stone crossing. It was not a line in standing water. It was not tested by water at all until 2 days later, when it was not in line, when it was in column on a causeway, and when what killed the men in it was not any failure of the rank.

To take a rule about standing water from the conduct of a column that drowned in a channel is not history. It is a quotation.

I have said this to the Office. The Office observes that the sixth issue is in print.

VI. WHAT I CANNOT ANSWER.

Two things, and I set them down because a case that admits nothing is a case nobody should trust.

The 4 words of the second day are 4 words, in a hand that wrote 4 words most days. *Line formed* may mean a line of battle. It may mean a line of march drawn up for inspection, which the same clerk uses the same phrase for on the ninth of the previous month, and I found that entry after I had written the rest of this and I have left the rest of this standing.

And I cannot produce an enemy. Not a name, not a body, not a captured thing, not one line in any Argonian account that admits a fight at the ford. The people who would know say the water did it and they say it consistently and they have no reason to be modest about a victory.

I believe there was a fight because a column stood to and I cannot think of another reason a column stands to. That is the whole of my evidence and I have written a book on it, and a reader who finds that thin is not being unfair to me.

VII. SCHEDULE OF THE DOCUMENTS RELIED ON.

I set these out because a case built on paper should say which paper, and because the day-book has never been printed and I would like the next person who argues about this to argue with the thing itself.

*A.* Day-book of the relief column, Ninth Cohort, leaves 7 to 12, held at Gideon in the cohort room. Six leaves. Two hands. Begins on the 9th of Second Seed and ends mid-sentence on the 14th. The first 6 leaves are lost and I have not been able to establish when.

*B.* Loss return, 3E 391, Office file, Claims (Accident). Waggons, teams, instruments, oil, rope. Entered throughout on the accident form and not on the enemy-action form, which is the single strongest document against my own case and I have put it in the schedule rather than in a footnote.

*C.* Casualty return, 3E 391. Two hundred at muster, 49 at the far bank, and no third figure anywhere.

*D.* Survey of the reach, third issue, appendix. Depth over the causeway in the dry season, below the knee. Volume of the weir ponds. It is on this arithmetic that Tribune Vell rests, and I accept the arithmetic and dispute nothing in it.

*E.* Office minute, registry 1114/9, raised by Undersexton Rell. On the authority for section 9 of the Standing Instruction. Two hands upon it and a third in the margin. I obtained a sight of this and I was not shown it in the ordinary way and I will not say by whom.

*F.* A muster leaf, torn, folded inside the cover of A, in 3 inks, giving a reconciliation that agrees with no published figure and reaches 42.

*G.* Deposition of Aneesha-Deem, taken at the Lilmoth customs house, unsigned by the witness.

VIII. ON DOCUMENT F, WHICH I HAVE NOT KNOWN WHAT TO DO WITH.

The muster leaf reconciles to 42 and says, in a third hand that has gone through the paper, that 42 is not 151 and that the Prefect and the Office were both told.

If F is right my whole account of the figures in section IV is not merely right but was already known at the time by the clerk who was doing the counting, and the received figure is not an error of arithmetic 36 years old but a return that was made up in the presence of a man who had the correct one.

That is a serious allegation to make out of a torn leaf in an unknown hand and I decline to make it. I record the leaf. A reader may make more of it than I have.

IX. ON DOCUMENT G, WHICH UNDOES ME MORE THAN ANY OF THE OTHERS.

Aneesha-Deem was above the crossing and saw the whole of the third day and was asked directly whether she saw any fighting on any of the 3 days, and answered no.

She was 14 and she was minding birds and she was looking at the waggons. She could not see the near bank from where she sat and she says so. It is not conclusive.

It is the only eyewitness in the file and it is against me, and every time I have set out to explain it away I have found myself doing the thing I accuse Vell of, which is arranging paper.

X. WHAT I WOULD LIKE, AND WILL NOT GET.

The first 6 leaves of the day-book. The whole quarrel is in what the column had been told before the 9th of Second Seed, and the leaves that would say so are the leaves that are gone.

I have applied to the Office twice for a search of the cohort room and have twice been told that the cohort room has been searched. It has not. I have been in it.

books.title: The Water Does Not Take Sides: What the Weir People Say About the Ford, Written Because a Prefect Has Been Asking
books.author: Neekus-Ei, of the weir households above the crossing, whose grandmother's cousin's people opened the gates
books.unreliability: She is answering a book she has been told about and has not read, and she assumes it says the cruder thing the officers who told her about it thought it said. Her account of the second day is her family's and is 36 years old and has been told at every gathering since, and she is aware of what that does to a story and says so, and tells it anyway.

contradicts.on: whether there was a fight at the ford before the water came

books.text:
A prefect at Gideon has written that we fought them at the ford and did not want to say so.

He has it the wrong way round, and I want to answer him, and I have not read his book because there is no copy of it within 4 days of here and I am answering what was read out to me by a factor who was pleased with himself. If I have his argument wrong, he may write again and I will answer that too.

WHAT WE SAY, AND WE HAVE SAID IT THE SAME WAY FOR 36 YEARS.

The gates were opened. My grandmother's cousin's people opened them. Nobody has ever denied it and nobody here has ever been ashamed of it.

We did not fight them. We have never claimed to have fought them and I want to be careful about why, because the prefect apparently thinks we are being modest.

We are not being modest. Nobody here could have fought that column. There were 200 of them with iron on and there were perhaps 30 of us at the weirs, counting the old and counting the young, and if we had come down to that ford with gigs and hooks the whole story would end in one afternoon with 30 dead weir people and a column crossing and going on inland.

That is why the gates. Not as a clever alternative to fighting. As the only thing available to people who could not fight and did not intend to be walked past.

THE SECOND DAY, WHICH IS THE DAY HE IS ARGUING ABOUT.

He says they stood to on the near bank for an afternoon and a night and that they would only do that if something was in front of them.

Something was in front of them.

We were in front of them. Not in a line and not with weapons out. About 20 of us, on the far bank, sitting down, in plain sight, at the top of the crossing where the stone comes up out of the water, and we sat there from the middle of the afternoon until it was dark and then we went away and in the morning we came back and sat down again.

That is a thing we do. My family has done it at that crossing for longer than the crossing has had an Imperial name. You go and you sit and you do not say anything and you do not go away, and it is not a threat and it cannot be answered and there is nothing in an officer's book about it.

Their officer sent a man down to the water 3 times. Each time we did not get up. Each time he went back. On the third time he brought bread, which was courteous, and we ate it, which was also courteous, and we did not get up.

So yes. They formed a line. Of course they formed a line. They had come 12 miles into a country they had been told was empty and there were 20 people sitting on a rock looking at them and their officer did not know what that was, and he had a book that told him what to do about an enemy and no book at all that told him what to do about people sitting down. A line is what you form when you do not know.

And then in the night the gates went, upstream, because the people at the gates had been watching the same 2 days we had and had made their own decision, and I will not pretend the two halves of my family did not know what each other were doing.

WHAT THE PREFECT HAS RIGHT, AND HE SHOULD KEEP IT.

He says a column that drowned in a channel on the third day cannot be used to prove anything about a line standing in water. He is right. We have watched their serjeants drill that line in the shallows below Hollow-Reeds and we have watched men go under in it in practice, in a training yard, with nobody attacking them.

And he says the 151 is a subtraction and not a count. He is right about that too and he is the first of them to say it. We buried a dozen. The rest went off downstream or went off overland and we saw them going, in ones and twos, for a week afterwards, and some of them we fed.

WHAT HE HAS WRONG, AND IT IS THE WHOLE OF HIS BOOK.

He needs there to have been an enemy, because an army that was stopped by 20 people sitting down and by a gate being opened is an army that has been told something about this province that it cannot afford to hear.

So he has taken *line formed* and made a battle out of it, and he has done it carefully and with real documents, and the documents are all real, and the thing he has built out of them is not.

I do not blame him very much. If I had spent 4 years in that room I would want it to have been a battle too. A battle can be lost and refought. What actually happened to them cannot be refought, and it has held this border for 36 years, and both of us know it, and only one of us can say so in print.

ONE MORE THING FOR HIS NEXT BOOK.

He asks why no Argonian account admits a fight at the ford.

There is a simpler question he has not asked, and I will answer it in case he ever does. Ask why the story we tell is about one woman and a gate, when there were 30 of us and 2 gates and a great many decisions taken over 2 days by people who all had names.

Because a story with one woman in it is a story your Empire can carry. A story about 30 people deciding something together, with no one to punish and no one to negotiate with, is the exact thing your Office has been unable to find a signatory for in 300 years.

We made the story small on purpose. It was the second thing we did that week and it has worked better than the gates.

books.title: Day-Book of the Relief Column, Ninth Cohort, Being the Leaves That Survive
books.author: kept by the column clerk, whose name is on none of the surviving leaves; recovered at Gideon
books.unreliability: The document both sides quote and neither has printed whole. It is a clerk doing his job in a hot week and it answers nothing, because a day-book records what a clerk was told to write down and a clerk is told to write down stores. The two entries everybody argues about are 4 words and 11 words long. It stops mid-line.
books.text:
*(The first 6 leaves are lost. What follows is leaves 7 to 12, transcribed at Gideon. The hand changes at the entry for the 14th and changes back for the last two lines. Spellings are as written.)*

**9th, Second Seed.** Marched at the second hour. 12 miles. Rd good to the second creek then not. Waggons 11, all up. Rations issd 1 day. Two men sick, one returned to duty. Water low. No incident to report.

Note: surveyors last message 9 days old, dated at the standing stone, asking for teams and rope. Prefect says we go on.

**10th.** Marched at the second hour. 9 miles, the road being what it is. Waggon 4 shed a wheel and was 3 hours. Heat very bad, 4 men down with it, all up again by evening.

Halted near bank. Line formed.

Rations issd 1 day. Nothing drawn from stores except lamp oil, 2 measures, which is not usual and I have entered it.

**11th.** Stood at line. No march.

Prefect down to the water at the fourth hour, at the sixth, and at the ninth with 2 loaves off the ration. Returned each time. Gave no order.

Men fed standing. Watch doubled. No wood cut on the far side.

Rations issd 1 day. 4 measures lamp oil. Waggons 11, all up.

**12th.** Water up in the night, no rain here.

Crossing begun at the third hour on the Prefect's order, column of 4, waggons in the middle as the causeway is narrow.

Surge at about the fifth hour. It came down the dry channel on the north side which had been dry when we came to it. I was on the near bank with the stores and I did not see the head of the column.

Waggons 11 lost with the teams. Instruments lost. Lamp oil lost.

I have been told to write 200 at muster and to write what came up on the far bank. I have not been given a number for the far bank and I am not going to invent one. There are men on this bank with me and I do not know how many and they keep arriving.

**13th.** No march. Counting.

I cannot make the count come right and I am going to say why in this book because there is nowhere else. Men are coming in from downstream all day. Men have gone off overland toward the salt hills without leave and I have watched them go and I have not stopped them and I would not know how. The Prefect is on the far bank with whatever is on the far bank and I am on this one.

If I write a number today it will be wrong tomorrow. I have written the stores, which I can count, and the stores are: rations 3 days for what I have got, oil none, rope none, teams none.

**14th.** *(different hand)* Column reformed. Return to Gideon ordered. Numbers as given by the Prefect: two hundred at muster, forty-nine at the far bank.

Clerk relieved of the book.

**14th, later.** *(first hand again)* I have got the book back for one line because I asked for it and the Prefect is a decent man.

The forty-nine is the far bank. It is not the living. I have got more than forty-nine here on this side of the water and I have said so twice and I have been told the return is made up and that it is not my

books.title: Office Minute, Registry 1114/9: Standing Instruction, Fourth Issue, Section 9 — Authority For
books.author: raised by Undersexton Aveline Rell for the Provincial Office at Gideon; minuted upon by two hands and not acted on
books.unreliability: A clerk asks a narrow, correct, unanswerable question and is told, in writing, in the politest possible terms, that the answer would be inconvenient. Nothing in it is false. The minute is filed under a registry number that was closed the same year, which is how it survived.
books.text:
**MINUTE.** Raised by the undersigned, for the direction of the Office.

**Subject.** The Standing Instruction for the Arming, Marching and Fighting of Auxiliary Cohorts, fourth issue, section 9 (the line in standing water). Authority for.

**1.** Section 9 requires that a shield line in standing water be held locked and that it be not opened in any circumstance, and provides for a file-leader who opens it to be broken to the ranks the same day.

**2.** The section's reasoning is given in one sentence, and I set it out entire because the whole of this minute turns on it: *"At the Drowned Ford the line held for the better part of an afternoon against a force that was never counted, and it held because it did not open."*

**3.** The Office has been asked by the Cohort's serjeant-instructor at Thorn to supply the authority for that sentence, so that it may be read to recruits with the returns beside it.

**4.** I have looked for the authority. I set out what I have found and what I have not.

**5.** *The engagement.* There is no engagement at the Reman ford in the returns for 3E 391 or for any year within 5 either side. I have searched the casualty returns, the honours file, the claims for lost equipment, and the Cohort's correspondence with the Office. The loss return for 3E 391 exists and is substantial and is entered throughout as a drowning. The word used in every document I have found is *lost*, never *killed*, and in the claims file the distinction is not sentimental: an item lost by accident and an item lost by enemy action are claimed on different forms, and every form in that file is the accident form.

**6.** *The force that was never counted.* No document in the Office names, describes, estimates or alludes to an opposing force at the ford. The Tribune's published account states that there was none. The province's own account, which the Office does not accept but which is at least a second source, states that there was none.

**7.** *The line.* The Cohort's day-book for the column does record, on the 10th of Second Seed, the words *line formed*, and records on the 11th that the column stood at line for a day without marching. The same clerk uses the phrase *line formed* on the 9th of the preceding month for an inspection parade. The day-book is at Gideon and has never been laid before the Office.

**8.** *Standing water.* The crossing is a stone causeway. The Office's own survey of the reach, third issue, appendix, gives the depth over the causeway in the dry season as below the knee, and it is on that survey's arithmetic that the Tribune's published rebuttal of the weir story rests. The Office therefore relies on the same document to establish that the water was shallow and on section 9 to instruct men standing in deep water.

**9.** *Conclusion.* The authority for section 9's reasoning cannot be produced. I do not say the rule is wrong. A rule may be right and its stated reason may be a quotation of something else. I say that the Office is instructing serjeants to break file-leaders on the strength of a sentence for which there is no paper.

**10.** *Recommendation.* That the sentence be struck from the fifth issue and the rule restated on the ground the Office actually holds it — that a line which may be opened at discretion will be opened by every frightened man in the province — which is an honest reason, is a good one, and can be defended without a battle.

*A. Rell, Undersexton, 3E 424.*

---

*(Minuted in a second hand, undated:)*

Seen. The Undersexton is correct and has done the Office a service and I have told her so.

The fifth issue is in print and at every station in the province. To strike the sentence now is to publish a correction, and a correction of that sentence is a statement by this Office that the Ninth was not engaged at the ford, and that statement will be in the province within a season and will be repeated back to us by people who have their own account of that day and would be delighted to have ours conceded.

The rule stands. The reason stands with it.

Recommend: no action, and the Undersexton to be thanked.

*(A third hand, in the margin, later, in pencil:)*

Sixth issue. Same sentence. Nobody asked me.

books.title: Deposition Taken at Lilmoth From a Woman Who Was Above the Ford, Concerning the Waggons
books.author: taken down by a clerk of the Assize at Lilmoth from Aneesha-Deem, who declined to sign it
books.unreliability: The one witness in the whole file who was on the ground and who is not arguing about anything, and she is used by both sides to mean things she does not say. She refused to sign because she was asked to sign a fair copy in which the clerk had tidied her answer about the number.
books.text:
*Taken at the customs house, Lilmoth. The witness attended of her own will, answered freely, and declined to sign the fair copy. The clerk records that she gave no reason for declining and that she was not pressed. Questions in the clerk's hand; answers as spoken.*

**Q.** You were above the crossing in Second Seed of 391.
**A.** I was 14 and I was minding birds on the bank above the second gate. I could see the causeway from where I sat.

**Q.** Describe what you saw on the third day.
**A.** The water came down the north channel that had been dry. It did not come as a wave the way people say it. It came as the channel filling, quick, the way a bowl fills, and then it went over the low place and out across the causeway sideways.

**Q.** Sideways.
**A.** Across it. Not down it. The men were walking one way and the water went the other way across their legs.

**Q.** How deep.
**A.** On the men, above the knee. Not to the waist. I have said that to people before and they get annoyed with me.

**Q.** Why should they be annoyed.
**A.** Because it is not deep enough for the story. Everyone wants it to have been over their heads.

**Q.** What happened to the men.
**A.** Most of them got off. They went forward or they went back and both were fine, it was 40 paces either way. The ones who went sideways with the water were not fine.

**Q.** How many went with the water.
**A.** I do not know. I have never known. I was 14 and I was looking at the waggons.

**Q.** Explain the waggons.
**A.** There were 11 and they were in the middle because the causeway is narrow, and a waggon cannot go forward or back when there is a waggon in front and a waggon behind. The men could choose. The teams could not. The water took the waggons off sideways one after another with the teams still in the traces and the drivers on them, and the drivers were the last thing I saw of most of them.

**Q.** You have said elsewhere that the loss was the carts.
**A.** I have said the loss I saw was the carts. That is not the same sentence and I have had it read back to me the wrong way twice.

**Q.** Clarify for the record.
**A.** The soldiers who died, died in the water going sideways, and I could not count them and I will not guess. The waggons I could count. There were 11 and 11 went. If a man wants a number out of me that is the number he can have, and it is a number of waggons.

**Q.** Did you see any fighting at the crossing on any of the three days.
**A.** No.

**Q.** On the second day, when the column stood on the near bank.
**A.** There were people sitting on the far side at the top of the stone. I knew some of them. Nobody fought. An officer came down with bread.

**Q.** Did you see the gates opened.
**A.** I was not at the gates. I was above the second gate with the birds and the gates are round the bend from there.

**Q.** Do you know who opened them.
**A.** Everybody knows who opened them. It is not a secret here and it has never been a secret and I am not going to be the one who says it into a book of yours.

**Q.** Is there anything you wish to add.
**A.** Yes. Every person who has come to ask me about this has wanted me to say either that the water was an accident or that the water was us. I have told all of them the same thing, which is that the gates were opened by people who could not have known what the reach would do, and that both of those halves are true at once, and every single one of them has written down the half they came for.

You will do it too.

*(The witness declined to sign. The clerk's fair copy renders her answer at question 12 as "the loss was the carts", and she required it altered before signature, and the alteration was not made, and she left.)*

books.title: Muster Leaf, Relief Column, Torn
books.author: unsigned; found folded inside the cover of the Gideon day-book
books.unreliability: A leaf of arithmetic in three inks that does not agree with any published figure, including the two it was presumably written to reconcile. Whoever kept it kept it folded inside somebody else's book, which is what a person does with a thing they cannot throw away and cannot file.
books.text:
*(A single leaf, torn along the left edge so that the first column of figures is lost. Three inks. The first two hands are neat; the third is not.)*

— at muster ......... 2 0 0
— sick, left at Gideon ... 6
— on the road ......... 1 9 4

*(second ink, below, ruled off:)*

far bank .............. 4 9
near bank, counted 13th .. 8 1
downstream, come in by the 16th .. 2 2
gone off ............... ?
dead, seen ............. ?

4 9 + 8 1 + 2 2 = 1 5 2

1 9 4 − 1 5 2 = 4 2

*(third ink, heavier, across the bottom, and the pen has gone through the paper on the last word:)*

42 is not 151.

They have got it as 151 because they took 49 from 200 and I have told the Prefect and I have told the Office and the return has gone.

I am keeping this leaf.
